summary.text: Climate proxies are preserved physical, chemical and biological traces of the past that stand in for direct measurements, letting scientists reconstruct earlier climates.
Reliable global climate records only began in the 1880s, so proxies such as ice cores, tree rings and corals are the only way to see climate patterns before then.
Most proxies are calibrated against measured temperatures while the two overlap, and that link is then used to work out temperatures from much earlier times.

items.prompt: A tree stump shows a run of very thin rings in the middle. What do those years most likely record?

options.label: Unusually good growing years
Hard years for the tree's growth
Years with extra strong sunlight
Years when it was first planted

items.explain: Rings are wider when conditions favor growth and narrower when times are difficult, mainly through temperature and water.

items.prompt: A scientist finds a new climate clue in lake mud. Before trusting it for temperatures from 10,000 years ago, what does she usually need to do first?

options.label: Find the oldest layer and stop there
Assume it matches today's climate
Count the layers to know their age
Check it against measured temperatures

items.explain: Most proxy records are calibrated against independent temperature measurements during their overlap, and only then used for earlier periods.

items.prompt: Why do scientists need indirect clues to learn the global climate of the 1700s?

options.label: Reliable global records start in the 1880s
Old weather diaries were all destroyed
The climate then was too stable to log
Early thermometers read the wrong units

items.explain: Reliable global climate records only began in the 1880s, so earlier patterns must come from proxies.

items.prompt: Ice cores often contain tiny trapped air bubbles. Why are those bubbles so valuable?

options.label: They show how fast the ice was drilled
They show where old storms began
They hold past CO₂ and methane
They keep the ice from melting

items.explain: The bubbles contain trapped greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide and methane, which help reveal past climate changes.

items.prompt: Researchers measure temperatures at many depths down a deep hole in the ground. Why can this reveal past surface temperatures?

options.label: Heat moves slowly through the ground
Deep rock keeps a written record
The deepest rock is always coldest
Groundwater carries old air downward

items.explain: Because heat travels slowly through the ground, the temperature profile down a borehole, adjusted for heat from inside Earth, can be turned into past surface temperatures.

items.prompt: A coral grew in the sea 500 years ago. Why might its chemistry tell us about the climate back then?

options.label: It keeps soaking up today's sea water
Corals grow the same in every climate
Its age alone sets its chemistry
That era's climate shaped it as it grew

items.explain: Each proxy, coral included, was influenced by a climate condition such as summer temperature at the time it grew or was laid down.
